title: Given an array of integers that may include negatives and a target k, find the length of the shortest contiguous non-empty subarray whose sum is at least k, returning minus one if none exists. Solve it with prefix sums and a monotonic deque and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: Challenge: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K (Prefix Sums with a Monotonic Deque)
keyPoints: The simple sliding window fails with negatives because shrinking can both increase and decrease the sum.
Prefix sums reduce the problem to finding the shortest span where prefix[i] - prefix[j] >= k.
A monotonic deque of prefix-sum indices stays strictly increasing from front to back.
Front pop: when prefix[i] - prefix[front] >= k, record the length and pop (no future right can give shorter).
Back pop: when prefix[back] >= prefix[i], pop (a higher earlier prefix is dominated by a lower later one).
Each index is pushed and popped at most once, giving O(N) total time.

s1_definition.oneliner: Use prefix sums with a deque that stays increasing; pop the front when the window qualifies, pop the back when a newer prefix is not larger.
s1_definition.profdef:
- This problem finds the shortest subarray with sum >= k in an array with possible **negatives**.
- The simple positive-only window **fails** because negatives break monotonicity.
- **Prefix sums** turn subarray sums into prefix differences: `P[i] - P[j] >= k`.
- A **monotonic deque** of indices keeps prefix values strictly increasing front to back.
- **Front pop**: qualified left endpoints are never needed again for shorter subarrays.
- **Back pop**: a higher earlier prefix is dominated by a lower later one as a left endpoint.
- Time is **O(N)** and space is **O(N)**.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh reviews intraday net cash movements that can be positive or negative and needs the fewest consecutive transactions whose total reaches at least a liquidity target. Because a negative transaction can sink a running total, the simple trimming trick fails. He keeps an ordered list of candidate starting points, discards any that are worse than a newer one, and confirms starting points from the front as soon as the stretch qualifies.

sections.s6_takeaway:
This problem asks for the shortest subarray with sum at least k in an array with possible negatives, and because negatives break the simple sliding window, you solve it with prefix sums and a monotonic deque in linear time. Prefix sums turn subarray sums into prefix differences, and for each right endpoint you want the latest left endpoint whose prefix is at most the current prefix minus k.

The deque maintains indices with strictly increasing prefix values from front to back. Two pops keep it correct: from the front, when the current prefix minus the front prefix is at least k, you record the length and pop (no future right can give shorter); from the back, when the back prefix is at least the current prefix, you pop it (a higher earlier prefix is dominated by a lower later one). Each index is pushed and popped at most once, so the total work is linear.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this on the intraday-liquidity desk. Net cash movements could be positive or negative, and the team needed the shortest continuous run reaching a required liquidity target to raise the smallest possible block of funds quickly. The prefix-sum-with-monotonic-deque method gave the correct shortest run in linear time.

The senior-level insight is recognizing when the simple window fails (the moment negatives appear) and reaching for prefix sums plus a monotonic deque. Being able to justify both pops is the proof of understanding: front pops because a satisfied endpoint is never needed again, and back pops because a higher earlier prefix is strictly dominated.

Remember one sentence: prefix sums plus a monotonic deque with front pops for qualification and back pops for domination finds the shortest subarray with sum at least k in O(N), even with negatives.
